b.x: The DEJEPS in equestrian sports makes you a state-qualified coach. It is a Ministry of Sport qualification at level 5 (bac + 2, two years of higher education). It lets you teach riding for pay and help horse-and-rider combinations progress in competition, up to Amateur level.
The pathway has three stages, all explained below:

it: The entry tests, to get a place on the course.
A safety check before you teach on your own on placement.
The 4 exams of the qualification, called UC, which you pass one by one at an approved training centre, often alongside work at a riding centre.

b.x: Some exams are on foot, others mounted: each section says which.
To start training, you provide two documents and pass three tests: two mounted and one on foot. You can take them in any order. To be accepted, you need a favourable opinion on all three.

head: Test
Mounted or on foot
Duration
rows: The length of the Amateur 3 Grand Prix test
20-minute session + interview of no more than 10 minutes

b.x: There is no mark. The assessors follow an official grid and give a "favourable" or "unfavourable" opinion, always explained in writing.

it: A medical certificate stating you are fit to take part in equestrian sports, less than a year old on the day you start training.
A first aid certificate: the PSC1, or an equivalent certificate recognised by the Code du sport (French sports code).

x.t: You ride the Amateur 3 Grand Prix test in a 60 × 20 m arena. Someone can call it for you. Your clothing and tack must comply with the FFE rules for Amateur competitions.
The assessors look at six points:

it: Your bearing, how you ride, your seat and how at ease you are.
How accurate your aids are.
How accurate your lines and figures are.
Correct paces: rhythm, regularity, forwardness.
The quality of the contact, the horse's outline and how responsive it is to the aids.
Impulsion and straightness.
Learn the test by heart, even though it can be called: you will be able to focus on your horse. The animated diagram is in "Review my tests".
Ride it in full at least once a week in a 60 × 20 m arena with the letters in the right places.
Work on every transition so that it happens at the letter, not a stride later.
Enter competitions at this level. In competition, each movement is marked from 0 to 10: the judges' comments show you exactly where to improve.
Have someone film you from the side and from the front: straightness and accuracy show up better on video than from the saddle.

x.t: You ride an Amateur 2 level course, between 1.05 m and 1.10 m, built to current technical standards. Your clothing and tack comply with the FFE rules. The elimination rules of the competition regulations apply: an elimination leads to an unfavourable opinion.
The assessors look at six points:

it: Your bearing, how you ride, your stability, your suppleness and how at ease you are.
How accurate your aids are.
Impulsion, a regular rhythm and an appropriate length of stride.
Your track: the quality of your turns and riding to the centre of the fences.
The jumps: keeping the horse between hand and leg, and the line.
The quality of the contact, harmony and flow.

b.x: The grid judges how you ride, not just the result: a clear round that is pulled about and messy can be judged less favourably than a flowing round with one pole down.

it: Jump full courses at 1.05–1.10 m regularly, not just single fences.
Enter Amateur 2 competitions to get to know the level in real conditions.
Work on your rhythm and your turns on the flat and over ground poles: they are what make a course flow.
Walk every course, counting the strides in the lines, just as you would in competition.
Have someone film you to check your stability on the approach and on landing.

x.t: You run a 20-minute flatwork session for 3 riders of at least Galop 5. An interview of no more than 10 minutes follows the session.

b.x: You choose your discipline from the 14 on the list: dressage, para-dressage, show jumping, eventing, driving, vaulting, western riding, endurance, horse-ball, TREC, hunter, mounted archery, pony games, working equitation.

x.t: The official grid for the session.
The assessors look at five points:

it: The safety of the riders, the horses and the people around.
How you use the space and lay out the arena.
How coherent your exercises are and how they link together.
Group management: keeping it lively and adapting the pace.
How you communicate to get the riders involved.

x.t: The assessors look at whether you judge your session honestly and whether your analysis is accurate.

it: Teach lessons before the test: it is the best preparation.
Practise running a 20-minute session with a stopwatch: an objective, a warm-up, two or three exercises that flow together, a cool-down.
Start by checking the tack and the riders' equipment: it is the first point on the grid.
Position yourself so you can see all three riders at once, and call each of them by name.
After each session, say out loud what worked and what you would change. That is exactly what the interview asks of you.
Ask a qualified teacher to watch you and give you feedback.

b.x: Once you are on the course, a safety check awaits you before you teach on your own on placement. It is done on foot, and a trainer from your centre assesses you.

x.t: You run a 20-minute group beginner session, in an outdoor or indoor arena, for riders from Galop 1 to 4. An interview of no more than 10 minutes follows the session.
The official grid for the session.

it: Making the working area safe.
Checking the tack and the riders' equipment.
Paying attention to how riders and horses are behaving.
Respecting the horses' physical wellbeing.
The riders' safety.

x.t: You can spot the risks in the situation and state the safety rules to follow.

b.x: With a favourable opinion, you can apply for your trainee sports coach card (carte d'éducateur sportif stagiaire).
The qualification has 4 UC. Three are on foot, one is mounted.

head: UC
What you need to be able to do
Mounted or on foot
rows: On foot: written file and oral
On foot: written file and oral, together with UC1

b.x: UC3 and UC4 are judged by at least two assessors who have held a riding qualification for at least 3 years. They follow a grid and give a favourable or unfavourable opinion, explained in writing. The regional jury then decides whether the UC is passed or not: there is no mark.
If you fail, you take a resit session. Generally, you keep the part of the exam you have already passed.
For UC3 and UC4, you choose a single discipline, the same for both, from the 14 of the teaching test. In driving, the UC4 demonstration is done driving; in vaulting, mounted or on the lunge.

it: You write a file of no more than 20 pages, not counting annexes. In it you analyse an experience in which you designed and coordinated a sports development programme.
You present it orally for no more than 20 minutes. You can use videos to support it.
An interview of no more than 40 minutes follows your presentation.

x.t: For UC1: your analysis of your yard's context, how you built your project and the resources you planned. For UC2: how you lead a team, promote your actions, manage logistics and monitor the quality of what you offer.

it: Choose a real project early on that you are running at your work-based yard: a clinic, competition preparation, a programme for a group.
Keep everything as the project goes on: schedule, budget, reports, photos, videos, results. These will be your annexes.
Write down what didn't work and what you changed: that is what shows your ability to analyse.
Rehearse your presentation out loud, with a stopwatch, in front of someone who asks you questions.

b.x: UC3 has two sessions, judged separately. You must pass both.

it: The assessors give you the theme, the level and the type of riders.
You have 1 hour to prepare and set up the arena. The riders are with you during this hour.
You run a session of no more than 30 minutes for at least 4 riders of Galop 4 or below.
An interview of no more than 15 minutes follows the session.
You watch an Amateur-level horse-and-rider combination for no more than 10 minutes.
In 5 minutes, you present your assessment and the objectives of your session.
You run a coaching session of no more than 30 minutes.
An interview of no more than 15 minutes follows the session.

x.t: Your ability to teach, to coach and to help each rider progress. At the resit, you can keep the session you have already passed.

it: For session A, prepare several sample session plans in advance, for each Galop level: on the day, you will only have an hour.
For session B, practise watching a combination for 10 minutes and summing up in one sentence what is holding them back, before suggesting anything.
Set just one objective per session, and check at the end whether it has been reached.
Have someone film you teaching so you can listen back to your instructions: are they short, clear and well timed?

x.t: It is a technical demonstration with commentary, in five stages:

it: You explain the technical difficulties you are going to show: no more than 5 minutes.
You show these difficulties mounted, at Amateur 2 level at least: no more than 10 minutes.
You analyse your performance and set work objectives: no more than 5 minutes.
You run a mounted work session while commenting on it: no more than 20 minutes.
A safety interview follows: 10 to 15 minutes.
Making the working area safe.
Checking the tack, how it is fitted and its condition.
Checking your own equipment: suitable clothing and a hat.
Paying attention to how the riders and horses present are behaving.
Respecting the horse's physical wellbeing.
The riders' safety.

x.t: You can analyse your session in a few words, show what you know about safety, spot the risks for yourself and others, and state the rules to follow.

it: Choose your difficulties in advance with your trainer, at Amateur 2 level at least, on a horse you know well.
Practise talking while you ride: describe what you are doing, why, and what you feel.
Before you get on, show that you are checking the ground, your tack and your equipment.
Prepare an honest analysis: what went well, what didn't, and the exercise that will fix it.

b.x: Your qualification or your competition results may exempt you from some of the tests, and sometimes from a UC. Exemption is never automatic: it is confirmed by the FFE's national technical director, on request with your supporting documents.

sous.titre: If you already have a qualification

head: Your qualification
What it gives you
rows: An older DEJEPS in dressage, show jumping or eventing
Exemption from the entry tests and the matching UCs
A level 4 state qualification that allows you to teach, such as the BPJEPS
Exemption from the teaching test, the check before placement and UC3

b.x: Other qualifications also give exemptions, provided you have supervised at least 300 hours in the last 5 years: the Animateur d'équitation, Degrés 3 and 4, the FFE level 2 coaching award (brevet fédéral d'entraîneur), and the CQP ASA, ORE and EAE.

Your placings can replace the mounted tests and, with better results, part of UC4. What is required depends on one thing: do you already have a teaching qualification (BPJEPS, CQP EAE or a level 4 qualification), with at least 300 hours of supervising in the last 5 years?
With a teaching qualification, good results exempt you from the entry tests, the check before placement and UC3:

head: Discipline
Exemption from the tests and UC3
Also exempt from UC4
rows: 3 placings in the top third, in Amateur 3 Préliminaire or higher
3 placings in the top third, in Amateur 2 Grand Prix or higher
5 placings in the top quarter, in Amateur 2 Grand Prix or higher (excluding special classes)
5 placings in the top quarter, in Amateur 1 Grand Prix or Pro 3 or higher
3 placings in the top third, in Amateur 2 or higher
3 placings in the top third, in Amateur 1 or higher

b.x: Without a teaching qualification, results only exempt you from the mounted tests, and you need slightly more:

head: Discipline
Exemption from the mounted tests
Also exempt from the UC4 technical demonstration
rows: 3 placings in the top third, in Amateur 2 Préliminaire or higher
3 placings in the top third, in Amateur 1 Grand Prix or higher
5 placings in the top quarter, in Amateur 1 Grand Prix or higher
5 placings in the top quarter, in Amateur Élite Grand Prix
3 placings in the top third, in Amateur 1 or higher
3 placings in the top third, in Amateur Élite or higher

b.x: The other 11 disciplines have their own criteria. To have your results recognised, ask the FFE for a performance certificate.

sous.titre: If you are an elite athlete

b.x: If you are or have been on the ministry's official list of elite athletes, you are exempt from the technical tests and UC4. With a teaching qualification, you are also exempt from the teaching test, the check before placement and UC3.
The FFE and the IFCE in Saumur also run a course reserved for athletes on the Élite, Senior, Relève and Reconversion lists. On this course, the teaching test is still compulsory.

sous.titre: How to apply for an exemption

b.x: You apply to the FFE on its riding careers website. Include your name, your licence number, your contact details and your official supporting documents. For a UC4 exemption, your teaching qualification must be registered on your licence.
If you have already been coaching for a long time, you can also obtain all or part of the qualification through accreditation of prior experience (VAE).
Plan your preparation over a full season. The tips for each exam are in the sections above; here is the order to work on them.
Compare your competition results and qualifications with the "Exemptions" section. No need to prepare for a test you are exempt from. If in doubt, ask the FFE before you start.
Work on dressage and show jumping at the same time, throughout the season, and enter competitions at both levels. Your placings may also count towards an exemption.
Start teaching lessons as early as possible: you need experience before the test.

it: Find the approved centres near you: they are listed by the regional authority (DRAJES) and on the FFE careers website.
Compare their test dates, their timetables (work-based, apprenticeship, continuing education) and their funding.
Find a riding centre and a tutor for your work-based training: many centres ask for a signed agreement before you start.

b.x: The DESJEPS, riding specialism, makes you a senior instructor (instructeur). It is the highest state qualification for teaching riding, at level 6 (bac + 3, three years of higher education), awarded by the Ministry of Sport. It prepares you to lead the teaching at a yard, train teachers and run a coaching programme.
It certifies 4 competences: building a yard's strategy, managing its people and finances, running a riding coaching programme and supervising riding safely.
The pathway has three stages, all explained below:

it: The entry tests, to get a place on the course.
A safety check before you teach on placement.
The 4 exams of the qualification, called UC.

b.x: Some exams are on foot, others mounted: each section says which.
To start training, you pass three tests: two mounted and one on foot. You can take them in any order, and you keep a test you have passed even if you fail another one.

Have a more highly qualified teacher film and coach you, in dressage as well as over fences.

x.t: You run a flatwork improvement session of no more than 20 minutes for 3 riders of Galop 5 or above. An interview of no more than 10 minutes follows.

b.x: Right at the start of your training, before any session with riders, your centre checks that you can keep everyone safe. You are exempt if you already have a teaching qualification.

x.t: You run a group session of no more than 20 minutes for 3 riders of at least Galop 7, in one of the teaching test disciplines. An interview of no more than 10 minutes follows, mainly on safety.

it: Making the working area safe.
Checking the tack and the riders' equipment.
Paying attention to how riders and horses are behaving.
Respecting the horses' physical wellbeing.
The riders' safety.

b.x: Each UC is either passed or not passed. The assessors give a favourable or unfavourable opinion, always with reasons, and the regional jury decides.

it: You write a file of no more than 20 pages, not counting annexes. In it you analyse an experience in which you designed and coordinated a sports performance programme in riding, including how it was evaluated.
You present it orally for no more than 20 minutes. You can use videos to support it.
An interview of no more than 40 minutes follows.

x.t: Choose a real project that you lead, with measurable targets, a budget and a team. Keep records of everything throughout the year.

b.x: UC3 has two exams.

x.t: Exam 1 — The video and its defence.

it: You make a video of no more than 15 minutes in which you train 3 to 5 BPJEPS or DEJEPS trainees: assessment, training or remedial work, then review. You add a written document of no more than 10 pages.
You defend them orally for no more than 15 minutes.
This is followed by an interview of no more than 15 minutes.

x.t: The assessors set the theme. You train 3 trainees in two parts:

it: In the classroom: no more than 30 minutes of preparation, then no more than 30 minutes of theory lesson.
In the arena: no more than 30 minutes of mounted preparation (setting up the arena, getting the trainees ready), then no more than 30 minutes of technical session.
This is followed by an interview of no more than 15 minutes.
Train trainees as soon as you can during your course, and film your sessions.
Practise making an accurate assessment in a few minutes, then building the remedial work.
Prepare short, illustrated theory lessons on the main teaching topics.

x.t: A mounted demonstration at Amateur 1 level at least, in a discipline drawn at random: dressage, show jumping or eventing. The exam lasts no more than 55 minutes.

it: You explain the technical difficulties you are going to show: no more than 5 minutes.
After the warm-up, you show them: 5 to 10 minutes.
You analyse your performance and set the objectives for a session: no more than 5 minutes.
You work the horse while commenting: no more than 20 minutes.
An interview on your session and safety follows: no more than 15 minutes.

x.t: The discipline is drawn at random: prepare all three, dressage, show jumping and eventing, at Amateur 1 level, and practise talking while you ride.

b.x: Your qualifications, your teaching experience or your competition results may exempt you from tests, and sometimes from UCs. These exemptions are confirmed by the FFE's national technical director.
Most exemptions based on qualifications also require 300 hours of supervising in the last 5 years. They include:

it: a level 4 qualification that allows you to teach for pay (such as the BPJEPS), or the CQP EAE;
the DEJEPS in equestrian sports;
the BEES 2, riding option;
an older DESJEPS in dressage, show jumping, eventing or equestrian sports;
FFE Degrés 4 and 5.

b.x: These must come on top of a teaching qualification and the 300 hours of supervising. Examples of results that count:

it: in show jumping: 5 placings in Pro 3, or in Pro 2;
in eventing: 3 placings in Amateur 1, or in Amateur Élite;
in dressage: 3 placings in Amateur 1 Préliminaire, or in Amateur Élite Préliminaire, with 1 placing in Amateur 2 show jumping or eventing;
in driving, western, vaulting and endurance: top Amateur-level results, with 1 placing in Amateur 2 show jumping, dressage or eventing.

b.x: If you are or have been an elite rider, you are also entitled to exemptions.
Exactly what each qualification or result exempts you from (tests, UCs) depends on your situation: ask the FFE before you sign up.
Compare your qualifications, supervising hours and results with the "Exemptions" section.
You need Amateur 2 Grand Prix in dressage and Amateur 1 in show jumping for the tests, and Amateur 1 in dressage, show jumping and eventing for UC4. Allow several seasons if you are not there yet.
UC3 requires you to train BPJEPS or DEJEPS trainees: offer to be a tutor as soon as you can.
